posts.caption: The hay guy delivers on Thursdays, and the good second cutting goes up in the loft before the rain so it lasts until January. I came back from the house with my coffee and found a small brown pony at the foot of the ladder, studying it like an engineer. He walked a slow circle around it, twice. Then he turned and looked straight at me. I moved the ladder behind the feed bags. He watched where it went. I'll be checking behind the feed bags every morning until spring.
posts.first: I grew up in a house where the good cookies lived on the top shelf of the pantry. My brother and I could always tell who'd been in there by where the kitchen chair was. Nothing has changed, except the cookies are hay and the chair is a ladder he can't climb.

posts.caption: The new gelding arrived Saturday in a trailer that cost more than my first truck. He stepped off with the confidence of a horse who has never heard the word no. By the time I finished the paperwork, the herd had sorted itself into a line, and he was at the end of it. He's very polite about it. He stands where he's told and eats what he's given. The round bale belongs to the draft mare, and there are four feet between him and it. I measured.
posts.first: The first barn I boarded at had a mare like that. She ran the pasture, the water trough, and the feeding schedule, and I was afraid of her for a full year. When I moved away she stood at the fence and watched my truck go. I still have the halter she wore.

posts.quote: The farrier arrives at 7:40. The horse knows by 7:38. Nobody has ever told him the time.
posts.first: My farrier has pulled into the driveway every six weeks for eleven years, and every six weeks my gelding has found something urgent in the back corner of the pasture. I've started leaving the lead rope on the gate the night before, as a courtesy. He has never once taken the hint.

posts.caption: The barn is supposed to close at nine, but it never really does. At nine the lights go off one at a time, from the far end back to the door, and I used to think it was just efficiency. Last week I stood in the tack room doorway and watched. She stopped at every stall and touched every latch. At the last one she stayed for a full minute with her hand on the switch. I went back to the house without saying anything. It didn't feel like my turn.
posts.first: My round bay mare's stall is the last one on the left, and the string lights over it run on a timer I set in 2017. They come on at four and go off at ten. I've replaced the timer twice and the bulbs more times than I'd like to admit.

posts.caption: We rode out at ten on the last warm Saturday of the year, with the leaves loud under every hoof. The old gray has been on that trail longer than I've owned the farm. He knows every stone, every creek crossing, and the exact fence post where the path bends back. About a mile out his ears came around and his walk got looser. I hadn't asked for anything. I just let him have it. We were back forty minutes early, and the hay was waiting.
posts.first: I used to be the one who wanted another loop around the back field. Somewhere around forty I started checking my watch on the way out. My husband says I've finally become a trail rider. I'm not sure that's what happened.

posts.caption: The first morning below freezing, my chestnut mare walked out of her stall looking like she'd been upholstered. Overnight, her sleek summer coat had become something you'd find on a good sofa. She stopped in the doorway and turned her head slowly in each direction, waiting. I told her she looked lovely. She didn't believe me, so I said it again. By lunch she'd found the one dry patch in the paddock and rolled in it, to even things out.
posts.first: I brushed out my own hair for forty minutes this morning and got about the same result. The mare supervised from the fence the entire time. Somewhere there is a version of me with a salon appointment. She isn't mad about it.
